fieldData.name: How to Build Pillar Pages for AI Search That Actually Get Cited
fieldData.meta-title: Pillar Pages for AI Search: Structure That Gets Cited
fieldData.meta-description: How to build pillar pages for AI search: what goes on the pillar, what goes on supporting pages, the linking pattern, and how to retrofit an existing library.
fieldData.post-summary: A structural guide to pillar pages for AI search: why retrieval systems reward clusters over single pages, the division between pillar and supporting content, the three internal linking rules, how to retrofit an existing library into clusters, a worked example from our own library, and how to measure citation share at cluster level.
fieldData.post-body:
Pillar pages for AI search are the page in a cluster that answers the broad question completely, with every narrow question moved to its own supporting page that links back up. AI systems favour the structure because an answer corroborated across several related pages on one domain is safer to quote than a single page making the same claim alone.

Most teams arrive at this problem backwards. They publish forty or sixty posts on a theme, notice that none of them is reliably cited, and assume the fix is a better individual page. It is usually the opposite: the pages are competing with each other, and no single one of them reads as the authority. This is a structural problem with a structural fix. If you want the mechanics of how models select sources before the architecture, start with our guide to what LLMO actually is. This piece is about how pages relate to each other, which is the part almost nobody writes about.

The Short Answer: What Pillar Pages for AI Search Do

A pillar page holds the definitive answer to a broad question. Supporting pages each own one narrow question that would otherwise bloat the pillar. Links run upward from supporting pages to the pillar and downward from the pillar to each supporting page, and never sideways between siblings.

The outcome you are buying is disambiguation. When a model retrieves three of your pages on the same theme and they each answer the same question slightly differently, it has no way to tell which is canonical, and the safest behaviour is to quote a competitor whose position is unambiguous. A cluster removes that ambiguity by making one page obviously the authority and the rest obviously its detail.

The vocabulary is worth settling, because two phrases get used interchangeably and mean different things here. When people say content clusters, AI visibility is the outcome they are describing: whether a system names you at all. When they say topic clusters, LLM citations are the narrower thing being counted: which specific page got quoted. You are optimising the first and measuring the second. This is not a new idea in content marketing. What is new is the reason it pays. Clusters used to be about distributing link equity for ranking. Now they are about giving a retrieval system several mutually consistent sources for the same claim, which is a different mechanism with different design rules.

Why AI Search Rewards Clusters, Not Single Pages

Retrieval systems do not evaluate one page in isolation. They assemble an answer from several sources and prefer claims that more than one trusted source supports. Google's own guidance on AI features in Search tells publishers to focus on unique, satisfying content with clear structure and sound technical access rather than on any AI-specific trick, which is a direct statement that the ordinary signals still apply. A cluster is the cheapest way to make the same claim defensible from several angles without repeating yourself.

The second reason is that the economics of a single page have collapsed. Pew Research Center found that users clicked a link on a results page in 8 percent of visits when an AI summary was present, against 15 percent when it was not, and clicked a source inside the summary itself in just 1 percent of visits. Being named inside the answer is now worth more than being clickable beneath it, and being named is a function of how quotable and corroborated your claim is, not of how much traffic the page used to earn.

Third, clusters are how you stop cannibalising yourself. Two pages targeting the same question split whatever authority the theme has earned. We make this argument about off-site signals in brand mentions versus backlinks in AI search, and the on-site version is the same: concentration beats distribution when the goal is to be the obvious source.

What Belongs on the Pillar and What Belongs on the Supporting Pages

This is the division most teams get wrong, usually by writing a pillar that is a table of contents with link text instead of an answer. A pillar that only routes is not a pillar, it is a category page, and models have no reason to quote it.

The Pillar: The Definitive Answer to the Broad Question

The pillar answers the broad question in full and stands alone. Someone who reads only the pillar should leave with a usable answer and no sense that something was withheld. It carries the definitions, the comparison table, the framework, and the direct answers to the two or three questions people actually ask first. It is long because the question is broad, not because length is a target.

Supporting Pages: One Narrow Question Each

Each supporting page owns exactly one question that a pillar cannot answer at depth without losing its shape: one platform, one tool, one error, one workflow. The test is whether the page has a question it alone answers. If two supporting pages would answer the same question, you have one page and a duplicate, not two pages.

The boundary to watch is overlap in the first paragraph. If the opening answer of a supporting page would also be a correct opening answer for the pillar, the supporting page is competing with its own parent. Narrow it until that stops being true.

DecisionPut it on the pillarPut it on a supporting pageWhy
A definition of the broad termYes, in the first paragraphNo, link up to the pillarOne canonical definition per cluster, or the model has to choose
A comparison table across optionsYesOnly if the page is itself a comparisonTables are the most frequently lifted element, so they belong on the page you want cited
Platform or vendor specificsA short section that links downYes, in fullSpecifics date fast and are easier to maintain on a page of their own
A step by step procedureThe sequence onlyThe full procedureProcedures are long and narrow, which is the definition of a supporting page
Troubleshooting one errorNoYesNobody searching the broad question wants one error message
Measurement and toolingHow to judge successWhich tools and how to configure themJudgement is durable, tooling is not

Internal Linking for AI Search: The Pattern That Makes a Cluster Readable

What follows is the pillar page structure 2026 rewards, and it is three rules, the third of which teams break. Link up from every supporting page to the pillar, using anchor text that describes the pillar's subject rather than the words click here. Link down from the pillar to every supporting page, once each, from the section that page expands. Do not link sideways between siblings unless the relationship is genuinely load bearing.

Sideways links feel helpful and quietly dissolve the structure. When every page links to every other page, nothing is above anything else, and the hierarchy you built exists only in your own site map. A crawler sees a flat mesh. Keep the graph shallow and directional and the shape stays legible from the outside.

Anchor text is doing more work than it used to. It is one of the few places you state, in machine-readable terms, what another page of yours is about. Our playbook for optimising content for LLMs covers the page-level version of this. At cluster level the rule is simply that anchor text should name the subject of the target page in the words a reader would use.

How to Retrofit Pillar Pages for AI Search Onto an Existing Library

Almost nobody builds a cluster from nothing. The real situation is sixty posts published over two years by three different people, with no structure and several accidental duplicates. The retrofit is a four step job and the first two steps are unglamorous.

Finding Your Accidental Duplicates

Export every URL and title, group them by theme, and then do the part that cannot be automated: read the first paragraph of each page in a theme and write down the question it answers. Pages whose opening answers are interchangeable are duplicates regardless of how different the titles look. This is tedious and it is the step that produces every later decision.

Choosing Which Page Becomes the Pillar

Pick on three criteria in this order: breadth of intent, existing authority, and commercial proximity. Breadth first, because a page that answers a narrow question cannot be widened without becoming incoherent. Authority second, since an existing page with links and history is cheaper to promote than a new one. Commercial proximity last, as a tiebreaker. Do not pick the page you like most.

Consolidating the Rest Without Losing Rankings

Merge the duplicates into the chosen pillar, keep the best material from each, and redirect the retired URLs to the pillar with a permanent redirect. Where a page is near-duplicate but has a real narrow question hiding in it, narrow it instead of merging it: cut the overlapping opening, keep the specific middle, and point it up at the pillar. Expect this to take longer than writing new pages, and expect it to be worth more.

A Worked Example From Our Own Library

We had the problem before we wrote this. DevCommX had five live pages on getting cited by individual AI platforms, one on ranking in Google AI Overviews, one on measurement, one on tooling, and a concept page explaining LLMO. Nine pages on one theme, each sound on its own, with nothing above them. A model retrieving three of them had no way to tell which represented our position.

The restructure named the concept page as the cluster's definition, kept each platform page as a supporting page answering one platform's question, and added a router above the platform pages so the breadth question has a single owner. Measurement and tooling stayed as supporting pages because they date quickly and are easier to maintain separately. Nothing was deleted: the work was deciding which page owned which question and making the links run in one direction.

The honest part of this example is what we cannot yet tell you. The restructure is recent, and citation share at cluster level moves over months, not weeks. We are measuring it the way described in the next section, and we will publish the result whichever way it goes. Anyone offering you a before-and-after number on a cluster restructure after three weeks is showing you noise.

How to Measure Whether the Cluster Is Working

Measure the cluster, not the page. The unit that matters is whether any page in the cluster is named when you run the theme's questions, because which page gets quoted is largely out of your hands and does not much matter commercially. Build a fixed prompt set of fifteen to thirty questions a buyer would actually ask about the theme, run it on a schedule, and record three things: whether you were named at all, which page was cited, and which competitors appeared beside you.

Establish the noise floor before you read any result as progress. Run the identical prompt set twice with nothing changed in between and record the spread between the two runs. Movements smaller than that spread are not results. This single step disqualifies most AI visibility reporting, and it costs one extra afternoon. Our guide to measuring LLMO and tracking AI visibility covers the full method, and the LLMO checklist and tooling comparison covers what to run it with.

Watch one failure mode specifically: the pillar earns citations while the supporting pages go quiet. That usually means the pillar absorbed too much and the supporting pages no longer have questions of their own. The fix is to narrow the pillar, not to promote the supporting pages harder.

Build Your Pillar Pages With DevCommX

The step that decides whether a cluster works is the one nobody wants to do: reading the first paragraph of every page on a theme and writing down the question it answers. Until that list exists, every later decision about which page becomes the pillar is a guess, and the restructure will reproduce the duplication it was meant to remove. We start there, then name the pillar on breadth of intent before authority, narrow the pages that are competing with their own parent, and set the noise floor before anyone reports a result. Our work on ranking in Google AI Overviews and on getting cited by ChatGPT are the page-level half of the same job. If you have sixty posts and no structure, send us the URL list and we will tell you how many clusters are actually in there.

FAQ

How do pillar pages for AI search differ from an ordinary pillar page?

The structure is the same, but the purpose changed. A classic pillar distributed link equity for ranking. Pillar pages for AI search exist to remove ambiguity: they give a retrieval system one canonical answer per question so it does not have to choose between several of your pages. That shifts the emphasis onto a quotable opening answer, real tables, and links that run in one direction.

Do content clusters help with AI search?

Yes, because retrieval systems assemble answers from several sources and prefer claims that more than one trusted source supports. A cluster gives a model mutually consistent pages on one domain making the same claim from different angles. It also removes the ambiguity created when several of your own pages answer the same question slightly differently, which is a common reason a model quotes a competitor instead.

How should you structure content for LLMs?

Put one canonical answer per question, open every page with a direct 40 to 70 word answer, and make the relationships between pages explicit through descriptive internal links. Link up from supporting pages to the pillar and down from the pillar to each supporting page, but avoid sideways links between siblings, which flatten the hierarchy into a mesh a crawler cannot read as a structure.

How many supporting pages does a pillar need?

There is no target number. The right count is however many genuinely distinct narrow questions the theme contains, which is often between five and twelve. Adding a supporting page that does not own a question of its own creates a duplicate and weakens the cluster. If you cannot state in one sentence the question a page alone answers, it does not need to exist.

Should I delete duplicate pages or merge them?

Merge rather than delete. Keep the best material from each duplicate in the pillar and redirect the retired URL permanently to the pillar so any accumulated authority and inbound links survive. Where a near-duplicate contains a real narrow question, narrow it instead of merging: cut the overlapping opening paragraph, keep the specific middle, and point it up at the pillar.

How long before a cluster restructure shows results?

Longer than a reporting cycle. Citation share at cluster level moves over months, and the honest first step is to establish your noise floor by running an identical prompt set twice with no changes in between. Treat any movement smaller than that spread as noise. Anyone promising a measurable citation lift from a restructure within a few weeks is reading variance as progress.
